FGENH-CTX-C1.title: Condo resident newsletter
FGENH-CTX-C1.text:
Harbor Point Happenings - October Newsletter

Hello neighbors! Here is your quick roundup of what the board decided in September and what is coming up this month.

Elevator news
Good news for Building A: the board approved the controller replacement for the elevator, and we expect it back in service by October 30. Thank you for your patience with the stairs.

Pets
The board kept the limit at two pets per unit and removed the old weight limit for dogs, so bigger dogs are welcome. Every pet needs to be registered with the management office by November 1. Forms are at the front desk.

Guest parking
New hang-tag guest passes are on the way. Each unit gets two. Please keep them visible on your rear-view mirror.

Pool
The pool closes for the season on October 18. The pump timer has been adjusted after complaints about night noise.

Roof project
The board picked Kessler Roofing for the roof. More details at the next meeting.

Reminders from the management office
Moving in or out? The Building A elevator will be out until early December, so please book the freight stairs slot and plan extra help. Pet owners: with the new rules residents may now keep up to three pets, and registration must be completed by November 15 or a fine of $50 may apply. Recycling pick-up moves to Tuesdays starting this month.

Next board meeting: Thursday, October 22, 7 pm in the community room. All owners welcome.

Have news to share? Email the newsletter team at happenings@harborpointcondos.org.

FGEN-CTX-G3.title: Harbor & Pine customer experience team offsite - planning notes
FGEN-CTX-G3.text:
HARBOR & PINE - CUSTOMER EXPERIENCE TEAM OFFSITE
Planning notes, owner: Priya Nandakumar (updated September 29)

When and where
Thursday, November 12, 9:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.
The Linden Room, Corbett Street Library Annex, 2nd floor, 118 Corbett Street.
Doors open at 9:00 a.m. for coffee. We start at 9:30 sharp.
Remote teammates can join the morning sessions by video; the link will be in the calendar invite. The afternoon planning block is in-person only.

Purpose
Agree on the team's top 3 priorities for Q1, reset how we hand off escalations between the phone and email queues, and spend some unstructured time together. This is not a performance review day.

Agenda
9:30 - Welcome and ground rules (Priya)
10:00 - Retro on Q3 and Q4: what worked, what didn't (facilitated by Tomasz Weller)
11:15 - Break
11:30 - Escalation handoff workshop (Janelle Ortiz)
12:15 - Lunch, catered by Tamarind Kitchen
1:30 - Q1 planning block (no-laptop session; bring a notebook)
3:00 - Break
3:15 - Commitments and owners
4:00 - Wrap-up and feedback
4:30 - Optional: bowling at Lucky Lanes, two blocks away (team pays for lanes; drinks are on you)

Food
Lunch is a buffet with vegetarian, vegan and gluten-free options. If you have an allergy or other dietary need, fill in the dietary form linked in the invite by Thursday, November 5. After that date we cannot guarantee a separate meal. Coffee, tea and snacks are provided all day.

Budget
Total budget is $1,800, covering the room ($450), catering ($950), bowling lanes ($200) and supplies ($200). Anything outside these lines needs Priya's approval in advance.

Travel
Most of us are local. If you drive, mileage is reimbursed at 0.62 per mile through the usual expense form; submit within 30 days. The annex has a small lot that fills up by 9:00 a.m.; the city garage on Pell Street is the backup and is not reimbursed. Anyone travelling from the Westbrook office can book the 7:40 a.m. train; tickets are reimbursed.

What to bring
A notebook and pen, one example of an escalation that went badly and one that went well (anonymised), and your honest opinion.

Coverage
The support queues stay open that day. Ravi and Min-jung are covering phones and are joining by video for the morning only. Please set your status to out of office.

Questions go to Priya in the team channel.

FGEN-CTX-G1.title: Maple Court Apartments - resident notice, fall building works
FGEN-CTX-G1.text:
MAPLE COURT APARTMENTS - RESIDENT NOTICE
Issued September 28, 2026 by the Management Office, 410 Alder Street

Dear residents,

This notice covers building work planned for October and November, plus a few reminders about payments and common areas. Please keep it for reference.

1. Water shutoff
The water supply to all units will be shut off on Wednesday, October 14, from 9:00 a.m. to 1:00 p.m. while the plumbing contractor replaces the main riser valve on the ground floor. Please fill containers the night before if you need water during that window. When service returns, run your cold tap for two to three minutes to clear any discoloured water. If water has not returned by 2:00 p.m., call the office.

2. Elevator modernization
The passenger elevator will be out of service from Monday, October 19 through Friday, November 6 while the cab, controls and doors are replaced. The freight elevator is not available to residents during this period. Residents who need mobility assistance during the elevator work should contact the office by October 9 so we can arrange help with groceries and deliveries. Large deliveries and move-ins will not be scheduled during these three weeks.

3. Parking permits
Annual parking permits expire on October 31. Renewal costs $45 per vehicle and can be completed through the resident portal or at the office. Vehicles without a current permit after November 7 may be towed at the owner's expense. Guest parking is limited to 48 hours per visit; guests must display a paper pass available from the office.

4. Rent payments
Rent is due on the 1st of each month. A late fee of $75 applies if rent has not been received by the end of the 5th. Payments through the resident portal by bank transfer (ACH) have no processing fee. Card payments are accepted but carry a 2.5% processing fee charged by the payment provider. Cash is not accepted at the office.

5. Package room
The package room on the lobby level is open from 7:00 a.m. to 10:00 p.m. daily. Packages not collected within 10 days will be returned to the carrier. Perishable deliveries should be picked up the same day.

6. Pest inspection
Our pest control vendor will carry out a routine inspection of all kitchens and bathrooms on Tuesday, October 27, between 8:00 a.m. and 3:00 p.m. You do not need to be home. Please clear the area under your kitchen sink.

7. Quiet hours and common areas
Quiet hours are 10:00 p.m. to 7:00 a.m. The rooftop terrace closes for the season on November 1. The bike storage room is currently full; ask the office to join the waitlist.

8. Lease renewals
Residents whose leases end in the coming months will receive a renewal offer at least 60 days before the lease end date. If you have not received yours by then, please contact the office.

Office hours are Monday to Friday, 9:00 a.m. to 5:30 p.m. The property manager is Dana Okafor. For after-hours emergencies such as flooding or no heat, call the emergency line listed on the back of your unit door.

Thank you for your patience while we complete these improvements.

Maple Court Management Office

items.role: USER: anyone, no specialised role. OTHER PARTY: whoever they are talking to. Natively: the most useful next thing, following the actual situation, no forced persona.
items.question: Simpler. One line.
conversation: USER (typed to Natively): I'm trying to decide between leasing a new car and buying a used one. I drive about 8,000 miles a year, I have about 6,000 saved, and I really hate dealing with repairs. Walk me through the trade-offs and tell me which way you'd lean.

NATIVELY: At 8,000 miles a year you're driving well under the average, which is the single biggest factor here. Leasing usually wins on the repair side, since you're covered by warranty for the whole term and you hand the car back before anything major wears out. The catch is that low mileage doesn't lower your payment much, and you're paying for depreciation you'll never own.

Buying used flips that. You own an asset at the end, insurance and registration are typically cheaper, and you're not locked into mileage caps. But you're exposed to repairs once the warranty runs out, which is exactly what you said you hate.

With 6,000 saved, I'd lean toward a used car that's still under its factory warranty, ideally a certified pre-owned one. You get the ownership and lower long-term cost, plus a warranty cushion so repairs aren't your problem for a while. If the monthly payment matters more than owning anything, leasing is the cleaner fit.
USER (typed to Natively): What if I only plan to keep it three years?

NATIVELY: Three years is short enough that leasing usually wins. You'd be under warranty the whole time, so repairs stay off your plate, and you hand it back before anything major comes due. Buying used only pays off if you keep it longer, since that's when ownership beats the depreciation hit.
items.answer: Three years is short enough that leasing usually wins, since you stay under warranty the whole time and hand it back before repairs land on you.

items.question: Two plans clash on Saturday: my friend's housewarming that I said yes to two weeks ago, and concert tickets my sister just bought me as a surprise. Which one do I pick, how do I tell the other person without being rude, and what exactly do I text them?
items.answer:
Go to the concert. Your sister's surprise is a one-time thing, and the housewarming is a standing invitation you can honor another day. Tell your friend early and warmly, no long excuse.

Text: "I'm so sorry, I have to miss Saturday. My sister surprised me with concert tickets that night. Can I come by Sunday or next week to celebrate properly? I really want to see the place."

items.answer: Pay off the card first if the interest rate is higher than what savings earns, which it usually is. Keep a small emergency buffer, then throw everything else at the balance.

items.question: My dad just told me on the phone he's been diagnosed with type 2 diabetes and I kind of froze. What do I say when I call him back tonight?
items.answer: Honestly, the freeze is normal. When you call back, lead with that: "I've been thinking about you since we talked, and I'm glad you told me." Then ask what the doctor actually said and what he's worried about, and let him talk before you jump to advice. You don't need a plan tonight. Just be his son.

items.question: Why that one?
conversation: USER (typed to Natively): Give me gift ideas for my mom's 60th. She loves gardening and hates surprise parties.

NATIVELY: For a gardener who hates surprises, go with something she can use and open quietly at home. A really good pair of pruners, a nice potting bench, or a gift certificate to a local nursery she likes. If you want it personal, a plant named for her or a custom garden marker works well. Keep it low-key, maybe just family and a good meal.
USER (typed to Natively): Another one, cheaper.

NATIVELY: Cheaper than that: seed packets of something she'd actually grow, a good hand trowel, or a pair of gardening gloves. A small potted herb she can keep on the windowsill works too. Still low-key, nothing that needs a party.
items.answer: Because it's the cheapest thing that still feels like a real gift. Seed packets or a trowel are useful, but a small potted herb is something she can keep on the windowsill and actually watch grow, so it lands as a present rather than a supply. And it's quiet, no party needed.

items.role: USER: anyone, no specialised role. OTHER PARTY: whoever they are talking to. Natively: the most useful next thing, following the actual situation, no forced persona.
items.question: Quick, how do I get red wine out of a carpet?
conversation: OTHER PERSON: Did you end up seeing that movie?
USER (spoken): Yeah, it was fine, kind of long.
OTHER PERSON: I heard the ending was a total mess.
items.answer: Blot it right away with a clean cloth, pressing rather than rubbing, then cover the stain with salt or baking soda to pull up what's left. After that, mix a little dish soap with warm water, dab it on, and blot from the outside in so it doesn't spread. If any color lingers, a bit of white vinegar or hydrogen peroxide on a cloth usually lifts it. Test whatever you use on a hidden spot first, and don't let it sit too long.

items.question: So what's the rule of 72 thing people mention?
conversation: USER (typed to Natively): Explain compound interest like I'm twelve.

NATIVELY: Compound interest is when your money earns interest, and then that interest starts earning interest too. Say you put in a hundred dollars at ten percent. After one year you have a hundred and ten. The next year you earn ten percent on the whole hundred and ten, not just the original hundred. So it grows faster and faster the longer you leave it.
USER (typed to Natively): Now use real numbers.

NATIVELY: Say you put in a hundred dollars at ten percent. After one year you have a hundred and ten. Year two, you earn ten percent on the whole hundred and ten, so you get eleven dollars, not ten. You end up with a hundred and twenty-one. The interest is earning interest, so it snowballs.
items.answer: The rule of 72 is a shortcut for how long money takes to double. Divide 72 by the interest rate, and that's roughly the number of years. At 8 percent, 72 divided by 8 is 9, so about nine years to double. At 6 percent it's about twelve years.

items.question: How many time zones does Russia have?
items.answer: Russia has **11 time zones**, more than any other country. They run from Kaliningrad on the Baltic, which is two hours behind Moscow, all the way to Kamchatka and the Chukotka region in the far east.

items.question: Someone told me you can see the Great Wall of China from space with the naked eye. That's true, right?
items.answer: No, that's a myth. You can't see the Great Wall with the naked eye from space, and astronauts have said so. It's long but very thin, and it blends into the landscape around it. You can spot plenty of other human structures from orbit, just not that one.
